GC.28.stem: Under the 'Tennessee Plan,' how do the state's appellate judges reach the bench?

choices.text: The governor appoints them, and they then face yes-or-no retention elections
They are chosen in contested partisan elections statewide
They are appointed by the President and confirmed by the U.S. Senate
They inherit their seats and serve for life without any election

GC.28.rc: RC-GOV7: Tennessee State and Local Government
GC.28.reteach: Re-read the Tennessee Plan description; contrast merit appointment plus retention with contested partisan races.

distractor_tags.label: B
distractor_tags.rationale: Right topic (judicial selection) but wrong method; the Tennessee Plan uses retention, not partisan races.

distractor_tags.label: C
distractor_tags.rationale: Confuses state selection with the federal appointment process.

distractor_tags.label: D
distractor_tags.rationale: Misconception that appellate judges never face voters; they face retention elections.

GC.28.key_rationale: The Tennessee Plan appoints appellate judges who then face yes-or-no retention elections.
GC.28.dok_rationale: Students interpret how a state selection process works, not just name it.
GC.28.blooms_rationale: Students explain the steps of the Tennessee Plan.

GC.29.stem: Because Tennessee is a unitary state, its county and city governments —

choices.text: are completely independent of the state government
hold only the powers that the state grants them
report directly to the federal government
may set aside state law within their own borders

GC.29.rc: RC-GOV7: Tennessee State and Local Government
GC.29.reteach: Re-teach unitary government and Dillon's Rule; use a chart showing authority flowing from state down to local governments.

distractor_tags.label: A
distractor_tags.rationale: Contradicts a unitary system; local governments are creatures of the state, not independent.

distractor_tags.label: C
distractor_tags.rationale: Confuses federalism levels; local governments answer to the state, not directly to Washington.

distractor_tags.label: D
distractor_tags.rationale: Misconception that localities can override state law; Dillon's Rule forbids this.

GC.29.key_rationale: In a unitary state, local governments have only the powers the state grants under Dillon's Rule.
GC.29.dok_rationale: Students interpret the consequence of the unitary model for local power.
GC.29.blooms_rationale: Students explain what being a unitary state means for counties and cities.

GC.30.stem: The Tennessee General Assembly is made up of which two chambers?

a House of Lords and a House of Commons
a Senate and a House of Representatives

formA.stem: A Tennessean files a lawsuit seeking an injunction and asks a court of equity to resolve a property dispute. In Tennessee's trial-court system, which court hears matters of equity and is presided over by a Chancellor?

choices.text: Criminal Court
Chancery Court
Circuit Court
U.S. District Court

formA.rc: RC-GOV7: Tennessee State and Local Government

distractor_tags.label: C

distractor_tags.label: D

formA.dok_rationale: Students match a scenario to the correct state trial court.
formA.blooms_rationale: Students explain which court handles equity matters.

formA.stem: A Tennessee city wants to create a new tax that state law does not authorize. Based on Dillon's Rule, what is the most likely legal outcome?

choices.text: The city may impose it because cities are sovereign governments
The federal government must approve the new tax first
The city cannot impose it, because local governments hold only the powers the state grants
The tax becomes legal automatically once local voters approve it

formA.rc: RC-GOV7: Tennessee State and Local Government
formA.reteach: Apply Dillon's Rule to revenue: a Tennessee locality may raise only taxes the state authorizes; test with additional 'can the city do X?' scenarios.

distractor_tags.label: A
distractor_tags.rationale: Contradicts Dillon's Rule; localities are not sovereign in a unitary state.

distractor_tags.label: B
distractor_tags.rationale: Confuses federal and state authority; state law, not federal approval, governs local taxing.

distractor_tags.label: D
distractor_tags.rationale: Uses a partly-true idea (voter approval) but ignores that the state must first authorize the tax.

formA.key_rationale: Under Dillon's Rule, a city may levy only taxes the state has authorized.
formA.dok_rationale: Students apply Dillon's Rule to a new revenue scenario to predict the outcome.
formA.blooms_rationale: Students carry out the unitary-state principle in an unfamiliar case.

formA.stem: In the Tennessee General Assembly, how is each individual Tennessean represented?

choices.text: by one state senator and one state representative, based on where the person lives
by two state senators and one state representative
by one state senator only, with no representative
by all 33 senators and all 99 representatives equally

formA.rc: RC-GOV7: Tennessee State and Local Government
formA.reteach: Re-teach the constituent concept: each Tennessean lives in one Senate district and one House district; practice locating both district numbers from an official source.

distractor_tags.label: B
distractor_tags.rationale: Right idea, wrong count; each person has one senator, not two.

distractor_tags.label: C
distractor_tags.rationale: Partly true (one senator) but omits the one representative each person also has.

distractor_tags.label: D
distractor_tags.rationale: Misconception about representation; a person is represented by their own district's two legislators, not the whole body.

formA.key_rationale: Each Tennessean is represented by one state senator and one state representative from their district.
formA.dok_rationale: Students interpret how district-based representation applies to an individual.

formB.stem: Tennessee copied the federal three-branch design but added its own features: the Grand Divisions, a part-time citizen legislature, and the Tennessee Plan. What do these three features have in common?

choices.text: Each was required by the U.S. Constitution
Each concerns only city and county government
Each is a distinctive feature of Tennessee's own constitution and government, not the federal model
Each was created by an act of the U.S. Congress

formB.rc: RC-GOV7: Tennessee State and Local Government
formB.reteach: Have students group the three features as 'Tennessee-specific additions' and explain how each differs from the federal design.

distractor_tags.label: A
distractor_tags.rationale: The U.S. Constitution does not require these state-specific features.

distractor_tags.label: B
distractor_tags.rationale: Right subject area but wrong scope; these are state-level, not only local, features.

distractor_tags.label: D
distractor_tags.rationale: Confuses federal and state authorship; these come from Tennessee law, not Congress.

formB.key_rationale: All three are distinctive features of Tennessee's own government beyond the federal model.
formB.dok_rationale: Students analyze what several state features share to identify a common trait.
formB.blooms_rationale: Students break down three features to find their unifying characteristic.

formB.stem: To identify the state senator and state representative who currently represent you, which is the most reliable source?

choices.text: a claim shared on social media
the official 'Find My Legislator' tool on the Tennessee General Assembly site (capitol.tn.gov)
a textbook printed several years ago
a friend's best guess

formB.rc: RC-GOV7: Tennessee State and Local Government

distractor_tags.label: C
distractor_tags.rationale: An old textbook may be outdated because officeholders change with elections.

distractor_tags.label: D
distractor_tags.rationale: A guess is not an authoritative or reliable source.

formB.dok_rationale: Students recall the correct authoritative source for a civic lookup.
formB.blooms_rationale: Students identify the reliable official source from memory.
